docs.openclank-docs-accounts-models.body:
# Accounts and Models

Sign in to the Open Clank account that owns your chats and journal pages. Connect a model for that account in [Settings](clank://settings) → **Provider/Model Management → Add Provider**.

## Connect a model

- **Local** connects to a model server running at an address Open Clank can reach. See [[Compare and Cookbook]] for serving a downloaded model.
- **API** takes a supported endpoint and its credential. The provider’s API quota and billing apply.
- **Subscription** uses a sign-in method offered by the provider. Model availability follows that account’s entitlements.

If **Provider login** is waiting, choose **Open current sign-in**. Enter the **Sign-in code** if offered. For manual callbacks, use the authorization-code field and **Complete login** on the original flow. Return to **Add Provider** or **Model Management** to resume an unfinished sign-in. Use **Cancel login** to abandon it. If the result is unclear, check Model Management before starting again.

## Check the inventory and use the route

In [Connected models](clank://settings/added-models), expand the connection and check **Models**. An empty list can mean the local server is unreachable, the API credential or endpoint needs correction, or the subscription still needs sign-in under **Account & advanced**. Use **Refresh models** after correcting it. A failed refresh can leave the last known list visible.

Select an available model in Chat. Its response label and [[Usage and Stats|Usage]] show which model answered. Switching models keeps the chat intact.

On the connection, **Disable** pauses the route and **Delete** removes the connection and its accounts. Use **Remove** on an individual account to detach it. On eligible models, **Share** lets you choose or remove named recipients. Models shared with you appear in Model Management.
docs.openclank-docs-chat-workspaces.body:
# Chat and Workspaces

Open [Chat](clank://chat), choose a saved chat or start a new one, and select a model. Attach files in the composer. For work in a Host folder, select the workspace and check its name before enabling **Shell Access**. Workspace rules, file permissions and individual approvals still apply. See [[Workspace Hexes]] and [[App Windows and Navigation]].

## Send or steer a follow-up

Enter sends and Shift+Enter starts a new line. During a reply, Enter normally steers the turn and Ctrl+Enter queues a new message. Change this in **Settings → AI Defaults → Chat input → Queue follow-ups by default**. Pending messages above the composer offer **Send now** and **Cancel** where available. Choose **Stop** to stop the active turn.

Hover over a colored mark beside the chat to preview a turn, or click it to jump there and enable its sound. Drag the grip above the composer to resize it; double-click to reset.

## See what the chat is using

In a saved workspace chat, open **Workspace**. **Changes** lists observed workspace edits. **Sources** shows attached files and sources from loaded messages. Use **+** to attach a workspace file or select a source card to open it.

Open **Sources → Model context** or the context meter. The meter can show an estimate for current context and a reported size for the last request. **Inspect provider frames** shows retained sources and model details by attempt, with gaps labeled. If offered, **Preview** a context selection before choosing **Apply selection**. See [[Agent Settings and Compaction]] and [[Usage and Stats]].

## Inspect a worker or a saved plan

Open **Workspace → Subagents** and select a worker to see its session, observations and available transcript. Use **Send follow-up** to address that worker when enabled. **Chat work** lists recorded commitments, executions and routines. Open a pending question or approval in the originating chat or worker.

In a chat with a saved plan, open the plan panel’s **Feedback**. Check the revision, save your comment, then choose **Send** or **Verify and send** to deliver it. See [[Tasks and Continuations]] for scheduled follow-through.

## Resume, fork or recover

Use **Chats** or `/sessions` to find a conversation and `/resume name` to open it. For a supported native chat, use `/timeline` to find a mapped user message. `/fork <host-message-id>` opens a separate continuation before it. `/recover` lists supported interrupted replies and gives the command to recover one. Reconcile a pending fork receipt before retrying. Type `/commands` for the browser command list.

## Preview or move work

Select **Preview saved HTML** on an eligible tool result. The preview lists dependency gaps and offers **Open in Editor**, **Export source bundle (partial static)** and **Widget state…** where available. Use **More → Copy Chat** for chat text or [[Search and Media#Keep or export an output|Review selected outputs]] for saved files.

In Files, select an eligible standalone Codex thread-history SQLite snapshot and choose **Preview selected history…**. Choose an **Owned workspace**, then **Preview threads → Open thread**. Select supported items starting with a user message. Enter a **New chat name**, then **Review import → Import selected**. **Open imported chat** opens the new chat for model selection. If the result is unclear, use **Reconcile import** or save the recovery selector for **File → Recover previous history import…** under the same account.

## Continue from a terminal

With the Open Clank CLI installed, open a saved browser chat and copy its ID from `/chats info`. Substitute your server URL and chat ID below.

```bash
openclank profile add work https://clank.example --use
openclank login --profile work
openclank run --profile work --session CHAT_ID --prompt "Summarize the decisions so far."
openclank tui --profile work
openclank logout --profile work
```

Approve the terminal in the browser. Use `--no-browser` to open the displayed URL yourself. The profile selects the server and `--session` selects its chat. In TUI, type `open` and a number from **Sessions**. Use `help` for commands and `quit` before `logout` revokes the credential. Without an OS credential vault, open TUI directly and authorize it for that process.
docs.openclank-docs-editor.body:
# Editor

Keep a source file, its reference image and your notes open in the same Editor. An image tab brings its own canvas, layers and history. Text tabs bring back your writing tools. Use **Text**, **Wiki** and **Graph** on Editor’s left rail to return to your files, read linked pages or follow their connections.

## Explore the workspace

**Explorer** is Editor’s file sidebar. With no folder selected it shows the places you can browse. Open a file to focus its workspace, or use **File → Open folder…** to pin a particular folder. Opening another tab keeps that folder in view. **Close Folder** returns to available places. The [[Journal]] shortcut opens your own writing workspace; the Instruction Manual opens its read-only examples.

## Source comments

In supported source files, native comments render Markdown, including images. Click a comment to edit the prose in place. Open its context menu and choose **See source** to edit the raw comment. Leaving the inset updates the draft. **Save** writes the change to the source file. See [[Source Editing]] for syntax selection and conflicts when another program edits the same file.

## Open and arrange work

Split a tab right or below from its menu to keep the reference beside the work. While **Text** is active, select its button to hide or reopen Explorer. **Details** follows the active document.

## Save, Undo and close

Editor and Wiki share a page’s draft and Undo history. If the disk copy changes while your draft is dirty, compare the revisions before reloading. See [[Recovery]] for an uncertain save.

## Media and source reveal

[[OpenClank/Files and Imps#Image projects in Editor|Keep an image’s layers]], [[Deliverables|review a recording or export a deck]], or select a rendered example in [[Markdown Formatting Demo]] to see its underlying Markdown.
docs.openclank-docs-files-imps.body:
# Files and image editing

Open an image from [Files](clank://files) to work on it alongside your text tabs in [[Editor]]. Files keeps its own location while Editor’s file sidebar follows the workspace you opened.

## Image projects in Editor

Crop or paint on the canvas, or choose **+ Import** to add another image as a layer. Layers and History belong to the active image. Pick the output by what you’ll need later:

| What you want | File menu |
| --- | --- |
| Reopen the layers for another edit | **Export layered project…**; reopen with **Import image project…** |
| Give someone the finished picture | **Download PNG** |
| Save a second image in Files | **Save as copy…** |
| Update the writable original | **Save file** |

**Open image draft…** resumes a retained edit. If the original has changed, keep your working copy and see [[Recovery]].

## Browse and open

Select saved HTML and choose **Open in Browser** for its preview. On a source folder, **Open in Code Graph** follows the saved files; on a file it starts with the containing folder. Missing host folders can be registered under [File access](clank://settings/file-access).

**Invite / manage access…** grants access inside the app. **Share download…** creates a download link. Choose a snapshot for a fixed version or a current-file link for subsequent changes. Revoke a link under **Manage shared downloads…**.

## Windows, split panes and views

Split a Files window right or below to keep the source and destination visible. Each pane has independent navigation. In a drag between panes, hold Option on macOS or Control on Windows/Linux to copy instead of moving. **Keep Both** retries a name collision with a new name.

## Create a file in Files

**File → New file…** creates the file in a writable destination. Choose **Open** in the receipt to go straight to Editor. For a personal [[Journal|journal page]], start in the journal workspace.

# Markdown Formatting Demo

Click a rendered block on this page to reveal or copy its Markdown. **Back to rendered** shows the result again.

## Task list

- [x] Mark the region in the reference image.
- [ ] Send the selected frame to the original chat.

## Quote

> Put the diagram beside the code that uses it.

## Emphasis and marks

Keep the **source**, mark the *draft*, cross out ~~superseded values~~ and ==highlight the change==.

## Table

| Keep editing | Share a copy |
| --- | --- |
| Layered image project | PNG |
| Workbook or slide deck | PDF |

## Links and references

[[Editor]] opens a manual page. [Settings](clank://settings) opens a control in the app. [[Wiki Recipes]] includes a live section embed.

## Code

```markdown
![[OpenClank/Editor#Source comments]]
```

## Footnote-style note

A source can stay beside its claim.[^source]

[^source]: Keep the version you used with the page.
docs.openclank-docs-getting-work-done.bo:
# Getting Work Done

Suppose an agent drew the wrong part of a reference image. Instead of describing “the thing in the corner,” open the saved image in [[Editor]], select the region and choose **File → Feedback on image region…**. The original chat receives a draft with the file revision and the region. Add the correction, review the recipient and send. [[Deliverables]] shows the same workflow for a chart, slide or moment in a recording.

Working on source? Give [[Chat and Workspaces|the chat a working folder]]. Open saved changes in [[Graph]] to follow a call back to its definition. If the next step belongs to you, keep it in [[Tasks and Continuations|Meatbag Tasks]]; if it should run later, schedule a Clanker Task.
docs.openclank-docs-graph.body:
# Graph

Open [Graph](clank://graph) from the Editor rail. In **Graph view**, choose **Journal & Wiki** to follow page links or **Code** to follow relationships in saved source code.

![Editor activity rail → Graph → Graph view. Journal & Wiki uses saved workspace pages and links. For Code, use File → Open folder… to select an authorized code folder, then expand a file to load symbols.](/static/docs/media/manual-graph-source-scope/preview.webp)

*Graph source diagram. Inspect saved links in Journal & Wiki. In Code, check index coverage before interpreting a gap in the graph.*

## Find a useful view

Filter by folder, kind, tag or property. Clear filters if the view is empty. Use **Structure** for a page outline and **Galaxy** for document and calendar relationships. For dated events, open [Timeline](clank://timeline).

## Try a small graph

Create **Field Notes** and **Reading List** in the same [[Journal]]. Add `[[Reading List]]` to Field Notes and save it. In **Journal & Wiki**, select the Reading List node linked to Field Notes to open that page. See [[Wiki Recipes]] for more link and embed examples.

## Code Graph

1. In Graph, choose **File → Open folder…** and select an authorized Host folder. Graph switches to Code. From Files or Editor, **Open in Code Graph** takes one supported file or folder. Confirm the containing folder if you started from a file.
2. In an Open Clank checkout, wait for indexing and open **View → Search & evidence**. Under **Indexed metadata**, find `atomic_write_text` in `core/atomic_io.py`. Select the declaration and choose **Show in graph**. Use **Source contents · literal** to find case-sensitive text in saved, indexed files.
3. Choose **Graph → Connections for selected item**. With **Calls** visible, choose **Trace from selection** in Inspector and select `atomic_write_bytes` as the endpoint. Choose **Open witness** to read the saved call site. Use **View → Graph table** for a text view.

### Expand a large folder

**Gravity** is the default for a new view. **Web** shows a network and **Map** a compact strip. In Editor’s Explorer sidebar, select a folder and use **Graph → Expand selected branch**. Choose **Load more for selected branch** if more results are available. Use **Hide selected branch children** to clear space.

In **View → Graph settings…**, choose **Gravity override** for a change specific to Gravity or **Common defaults** for all layouts.

| What you need | Where to adjust it |
| --- | --- |
| Load more of a branch | **Paging & expansion** controls read size and depth. |
| Keep or show more of what is loaded | **Map cache** bounds what Graph retains. **Display capacity** bounds what it draws. Check **Effective capacity** for the limits in use. |
| Include more source files | **Settings → System → Code indexing** sets file and byte limits. |
| Make a crowded view readable | Use **Labels & relationships** to isolate calls or imports and **Motion & camera** to reduce animation. Save grouping and spacing under **Named physics settings**. |

### Resolve a partial or stale graph

Folder structure can appear before symbol evidence is ready. If a branch is missing, check **View → Coverage and diagnostics** for index coverage, then clear filters or load more. After a source save, use **Graph → Refresh now** if the old view is still showing. Use **Retry indexing** or **Readmit erased index** when offered.

### Review and share evidence

Open a call witness for the saved source behind a static edge. Inferred edges reflect source rules. **Recorded changes** shows observed file activity, and eligible static-function views can open **Imported trace evidence**. Open a trace there to inspect the observations it contains.

Choose **Add selected evidence to chat** to put it in the draft or **Ask about selected evidence** to send a question. In **Search & evidence**, use **Summarize selected evidence → Preview** to review the source scope and model before generating. Check the finished summary against its source links. To save a fact for future recall, see [[Memory and Lore]].

Use **File → Export current graph…** to preview the displayed graph and omissions. Choose a format and **Save**, or **Create new wiki document…** when offered. Reopen the preview if the graph changes.

## Official pages

Use **Include official documentation** to show handbook pages.
docs.openclank-docs-home.body:
# Open Clank

Open Clank is a self-hosted AI workspace for turning ideas into finished work. Your personal agent works with your notes and files from day one.

[[Journal|Copal]] is an open-source alternative to Obsidian. Its built-in [[Editor|file editor]] handles text, code and images. [[Graph]] maps links between journal pages, dependencies in your workspace and the files your notes refer to.

Learn in [[TreeHouse]], a pre-alpha learning management suite. Track milestones on [Timeline](clank://timeline), [[Tasks and Continuations|schedule tasks]] and [[Calendar and Email|sync your calendar]].

![Editor activity rail → Graph → Graph view. Journal & Wiki uses saved workspace pages and links. For Code, use File → Open folder… to select an authorized code folder, then expand a file to load symbols.](/static/docs/media/manual-graph-source-scope/preview.webp)

*Graph source diagram. Inspect saved links in Journal & Wiki. In Code, check index coverage before interpreting a gap in the graph.*

[[Accounts and Models|Connect your first model]] · [[Chat and Workspaces|Start a project chat]] · [[Manual Index|Browse the manual]]
docs.openclank-docs-home.title: Instruction Manual
docs.openclank-docs-limits.body:
# Limits and Platform Support

Check your exact package and checksum. [Beta 2 release and artifact records](https://github.com/Plaer1/open-clank/releases/tag/v1.0.3-beta.2).

| Platform | Support |
| --- | --- |
| macOS | Apple Silicon package for macOS 15 or later. Ad-hoc signed. |
| Windows | Use an architecture offered by the release. Installed-package checks are recorded per artifact. |
| Linux | Source setup is documented. App and package qualification remain open. |
| Docker | Legacy files. Unsupported. |

For installation steps see [[Setup and First Run]]. For source and package evidence see the [known limits](https://github.com/Plaer1/open-clank/blob/main/clank-code/docs/known-limits.md).

## What depends on my installation?

- **Host actions** depend on OS access and available handlers. See [[Desktop Capture and Host Opening]].
- [[Graph|Code Graph]] shows the evidence for each indexed relationship. Check coverage when a call or dependency is missing.
- **Remote services** receive the material you send and may charge for requests. Model and provider capabilities vary. See [[Accounts and Models]].
- **Journal** uses Files-backed storage in the current hosted app. Preserve older stores using the upgrade and backup guides before switching. See [[Recovery]].

The service runs within its host OS account’s permissions. A link follows the reader’s existing grants. [Deployment security](https://github.com/Plaer1/open-clank/blob/main/.github/SECURITY.md).
docs.openclank-docs-limits.title: Limits and Platform Support
docs.openclank-docs-memory-lore.body:
# Memory and Lore

| If you need… | Open… |
| --- | --- |
| What was said or which tools ran | The original chat or transcript |
| A fact or preference the assistant can recall | [Memery](clank://memory) |
| Reported or estimated token counts | [[Usage and Stats]] |
| An earlier state of a file | The project's or document's History |

## Semantic memory

To save a preference, open **Memery → Add → Add Memory**, type it, select a category and press Enter. If it goes to review, open **Inspect → Candidates → Pending**. Check the wording and source, then **Edit**, **Promote**, or **Reject**. Promoted entries appear under **Curated**. Other profiles save the entry directly in **Memories**.

In **Inspect**, **Raw trajectory** shows captured evidence, **History** shows revisions, and **Quarantined** shows items withheld from recall. For eligible pending additions, use **Select for atomic batch** to preview and approve several together. If the result is unknown, choose **Check original status**.

To correct an outdated claim, open the newer item in **Memories → … → Details → Review relationship**. Choose the earlier item or **Find suggested pairs**. Use **Compare evidence** to read both claims and their sources. Choose **Preview supersession → Confirm supersession** or **Decline pair**. **Detach** removes a confirmed link while keeping both histories.

## Review an import batch

Use **Add → Add Memory → Import** to select files. When processing finishes, open **review** on the banner in **Memories**. Check suggestions against their sources and edit, save or reject each one. Use **check import status** for files that need attention.

Use **Export as Markdown** for one file or **Export as Markdown files (zip)** for separate files in a ZIP. When you import an Open Clank Markdown export, the text goes through review.

## Move reviewed knowledge

1. From a memory's **…** menu, choose **Export knowledge snapshot…**. Preview the full text and category before **Confirm and download**. For several memories, use **Select → Export selected as snapshots…** and check the included count.
2. In the receiving account, choose **Add → Add Memory → Import snapshot…** or **Import snapshot bundle…**. Use **Preview** for a single file or **Start import** for a bundle. Read the text and category and choose **Create review draft** for each item you want.
3. In **Memories → review**, decide which drafts to retain. Inspect skipped or refused bundle items and preview again if the bytes change. Check the original status for an unknown outcome.

For a saved folder analysis, choose **Check original files** on the memory. Select the original Host folder under its owned workspace. **Compare saved snapshot** reports the result for each component, including any it could not verify.

## Skills, prompts and admission

1. Open **Add → Add Skill → Marketplace…** and choose an offered source. Select **Preview catalog → View components → Review skill** for the skill you want. Review the publisher, release and files before **Create draft**.
2. In **Skills**, open the draft, read the instructions and companion files, then **Publish** to make it available. **Settings → Inject Skills** controls how many relevant skills can join a request. Zero turns off automatic injection.
3. In chat, expand **Skill used: …** to see the loaded revision and files when a receipt is available. To withdraw a skill, choose **Unpublish** on its card.

To move a published skill, use **Export snapshot…**, preview its contents and download it. Use **Add Skill → Import snapshot…** in the receiving account to review and create an independent draft.

## Timeline and Graph

**Memery → Graph** shows memory relationships. [[Graph]] follows links between journal pages or saved source. For an open chat, **Inspect → Journal coverage** shows chat consolidation progress. On a synthesis candidate, use **Review Journal sources → Open source chat** to review its citations. Open [[Journal]] for personal pages.

## Lore and recovery

Use the document's or project's **History** to inspect earlier file states before restoring. See [[Recovery]] for file restoration and pending operations.

**Settings → Nuke my Brain data** previews removal of selected live Memery data. Review the chosen categories and result. Source files, exports and backups are retained separately.
docs.openclank-docs-memory-lore.title: Memory and Lore
docs.openclank-docs-recovery.body:
# Recovery

Keep your draft until you know what was saved.

| Problem | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Save conflict | Reopen the stored revision and merge your draft. |
| Save refused because a recovery version is unavailable | Restore the recovery service before retrying. |
| Editor cannot read a document | Inspect the preserved source or restore an earlier version. Preserve the original bytes. |
| Missing file or media | Check the account and **Permissions → Your file access**. Relink a moved resource or replace an expired link with a saved file. |
| Unsure whether an external action finished | Check the original result or receipt before repeating the action. |
| Handbook page changed | Reopen it from Help for the current edition. Your personal notes stay in their own documents. |
| Missing sidebar shortcut | Restore it in **Settings → Appearance → Copal navigation**. |

## Restore a file or project

Select the file, then choose **Actions → History** to review its versions or checkpoints. For an open Host folder, choose **Go → Folder History…** and open a file’s versions from the recorded changes or **Removed files**. Review the selected version before confirming a restore. See [[Memory and Lore]].

## Restore an installation

The repository backup helper covers its `data/` directory. Check for Journal storage, host workspaces and other stores outside that directory. **Settings → System → Data Backup** transfers the listed user-data categories as JSON. For full restore steps and coverage, use the [backup guide](https://github.com/Plaer1/open-clank/blob/main/clank-code/docs/backup-restore.md).
docs.openclank-docs-recovery.title: Recovery
docs.openclank-docs-settings-themes.body:
# Settings and Themes

Use **Find a setting…** to jump to a control. Theme and keyboard bindings are browser-local. Provider connections and launcher visibility belong to your account. [Settings](clank://settings).

## Files, Editor and agent access

**Permissions → Your file access** shows what you can open in Files and Editor. Administrators share a **Location** through **People**, with **Browse / download** or **Modify** access. **Operation approvals** shows saved agent approvals and when they expire.

The owner and administrators can set **Permissions → Full filesystem access** for their own accounts. **Files and Editor** and **Agents for this account** are separate switches. On uses the host OS account’s permissions. Off uses existing folder grants. **Account → Full access** enables models and optional tools where offered.

## Account and administration

Set up your authenticator under **Account → Two-Factor Authentication**. For a provider login, see [[Accounts and Models]]. Administrators manage scoped API tokens at `/api/tokens`.

Check **Logging → Storage inventory**, or use the administrator’s **System → Stack health**, **Terminal Logs** and **Data Backup**. For what backups cover, see [[Recovery#Restore an installation|Restore an installation]].

**Tokenomics** lets you opt into changes such as reusing exact repeated Browser snapshot text. Check the effective settings there and observed usage under [[Usage and Stats]].

## Connect an MCP tool server

As an administrator, open **Settings → Integrations → MCP Tool Server**. Select **stdio** for a command, arguments and environment on the host, or **SSE** or **Streamable HTTP** for a server URL. Put credentials in the connection settings. Choose **Save**, complete **Authorize** if prompted and check the tool list. A local command uses the host’s access. A remote tool receives the data you pass to it.

## Change appearance

Open [Appearance](clank://settings/appearance). Choose **Solid** to stop background motion. **Copal navigation** restores a hidden Journal shortcut. [Shortcuts](clank://settings/shortcuts) shows your bindings.

Choose **Interface language** here to switch the controls and the built-in handbook. Your own messages and documents keep their original text.

New supported workbooks and decks use the current theme. To change an existing one, see [[Deliverables#Edit a slide deck|Apply the current theme]]. **Reduce motion in generated deliverables** is an account preference.

## Google Emoji Drift artwork

Select **Emoji Drift** to review consent. Regular emoji appear immediately and give way to downloaded artwork as it arrives. **Allow** permits acquisition. Choose **Refresh artwork status** under Emoji Drift to see download and update progress, pause or resume weekly updates, or **Revoke emoji artwork consent**. See [[Credits and Included Components]].
docs.openclank-docs-tasks.body:
# Tasks and Continuations

Open [Tasks](clank://tasks). **Meatbag Tasks** holds work you follow through on. **Clanker Tasks** runs model work on a schedule or on demand. **Workload** shows the commitments, executions and routines the current scope recorded.

## Track your own work

In **Meatbag Tasks**, create an item, check its title, source and due date, and mark it complete when done. A page checklist stays in the page until you use an explicit task action that creates an item in Tasks.

## Schedule or continue model work

In **Clanker Tasks → New Task**, set the prompt, model, schedule and output destination. Verify access to that destination. A task with email delivery can send to the saved address. Save and check the next-run time, or use **Run now**.

Use the task log to inspect or stop the current run. **History** shows prior output or errors. Check the previous outcome before retrying a task that can send or modify something. **Pause** and **Resume** control its schedule.

In Chat, ask explicitly for a task when the work needs its own schedule or record. Open the resulting task chat to answer its question. Follow an existing worker from **Workload** or [[Chat and Workspaces#Inspect a worker or a saved plan|the chat’s worker view]].

## Review repository changes

Open the repository root in Files and select its managed chat. Choose **Files → Go → Git workbench…** to see working and staged changes. Choose a file if required, select a **Git operation**, then use **Review** to inspect the saved bytes and target before confirming. If the result is pending, use **Check status**. See [[Recovery]] for file history.
docs.openclank-docs-tasks.title: Tasks and Continuations
treehouse.class.house-collaborate.descri: Open Clank assumes you already know how to talk to an assistant. These lessons cover what is distinctive here: account-aware models, chats that keep their identity across workspaces, inspectable tool activity, durable goals with evidence, scheduled work that answers in its own task chat, and two different kinds of memory.
treehouse.class.house-collaborate.summar: Models, chat identity, tool authority, goals, schedules and the difference between Memery and Lore.
treehouse.class.house-collaborate.title: Work With Your Clanker
treehouse.class.house-connections.descri: The value of a document grows with what it is connected to. These lessons cover link navigation, the Graph's two document modes, programmatic filters, Bases over typed content, tasks and timeline entries that point back at their source, and research notes that keep their sources.
treehouse.class.house-connections.summar: Links, Graph modes, filters and camera, Bases, source-backed tasks and Timeline, and attributable research.
treehouse.class.house-connections.title: Follow the Threads
treehouse.class.house-documents.descript: Documents in Open Clank are not a notepad. They hold template sections, linked Wiki pages, typed tables with real formulas, comment regions over programming source, and images that stay attached to the document that references them.
treehouse.class.house-documents.summary: Documents, templates, splits, rich source comments, typed tables, Wiki pages and attached images.
treehouse.class.house-documents.title: Documents With Teeth
treehouse.class.house-making.description: Making things in Open Clank means files you can move, images you can edit without losing the original, exports you can hand to someone else, and recovery that actually restores. These lessons are the workshop.
treehouse.class.house-making.summary: Files and workspaces, clipboard media, Imps editing, project export, Lore restore and scoped exports.
treehouse.class.house-making.title: Make, Move, Recover
treehouse.class.house-stewardship.descri: The house works better when it fits you. These lessons cover the maintained handbook, appearance and accessibility controls that live in Settings, app links that take you where the text points, local drafts for email and calendar, making a Class to teach someone else, and reading your own progress honestly.
treehouse.class.house-stewardship.summar: Official docs, theme and accessibility, app links, local drafts, authoring a Class, and reading your progress.
treehouse.class.house-stewardship.title: Make the House Yours
treehouse.lesson.house-collaborate.chat-:
Open [Chat](clank://chat) and send one message. Switch to a different workspace (or open a different project), then return to the chat list and reopen the same conversation. The transcript is intact and the session is the same one.

**Observable result:** the chat reopens with the same session identity and the earlier turns still visible. Opening a lesson never starts a model call; sending a message is the paid action and it is always yours to send.

A chat is bound to a session identity, not to the folder you were looking at. Change workspace and the chat keeps its session ID and transcript. Work context changes; the conversation does not silently become a different one.
Nothing to delete. The chat is your own normal conversation.
The same chat reopens with its earlier turns after the workspace change.
Send any single message, then switch workspace and reopen this chat.
The same chat reopened in a different workspace, still recognisably itself.
A chat that keeps its identity when the workspace changes

This is what makes it safe to organise work into workspaces without losing the thread of a conversation. Your follow-up questions still land in the same chat, and the answer still knows what came before.
treehouse.lesson.house-collaborate.durab:
Open [Chat](clank://chat) on a session and create a goal with a concrete requirement — for example, "produce a summary and attach it as a document." Work toward it. When the work is done, verify the goal; verification needs the goal's identity and revision plus the evidence you named.

**Observable result:** the goal reaches a verified completed state with its evidence references satisfied. A model statement alone cannot complete it.

A durable goal is more than a to-do. It records what must be true, and completing it requires the evidence you asked for — not a model saying "done." Goals live with the session and survive the turn that created them.
Complete or dismiss the goal normally; it is ordinary session state.
The goal shows a verified completed state with its evidence reference recorded.
Create one goal whose completion requires a named document or artifact as evidence.
A goal that carries its own requirement for proof before it is called done.
This is the difference between work that looks finished and work you can check. When the goal demands evidence, the verification is yours to review, not a claim to trust.
treehouse.lesson.house-collaborate.menme:
Open [Memery](clank://memory) and review a pending candidate — accept one you actually want. Then search for a record and open it. Separately, open a document's history and look at the retained versions; those are Lore's material.

Retention budgets live in [Settings → History](clank://settings/history). What is not retained cannot be restored.

**Memery** is the sidebar where memory lives: candidates waiting for your review, and search over what you kept. You accept a candidate explicitly; nothing is written behind your back. **Lore** is recovery: retained versions of your work and the receipts that let you restore them.
Two different tools, used for two different jobs.
Memery review and recall versus Lore recovery
Confusing the two wastes time. Memery answers "what does the assistant know about me?" Lore answers "how do I get yesterday's version back?" Review is about the future; restore is about the past.
treehouse.lesson.house-collaborate.model:
Open [Settings → Providers](clank://settings/providers) and note which model is the Default Chat Model. Then open [Chat](clank://chat) and write a brief for something you actually need: name the outcome, the audience and one constraint. Send it on the model you chose.

**What is distinctive:** the model is an account setting, not a hidden global. Providers you add are yours; the same settings panel shows which ones are configured.

Models are configured per account in [Settings → Providers](clank://settings/providers). The Default Chat Model is what a new chat uses; Deep Research and other specialised work can inherit it or set their own. A provider is the service behind a model — add one and its models become selectable.
A chat opened with the model you chose and a brief that names the outcome you want.
Account-aware models and a useful brief

Choosing the model deliberately is the difference between a cheap draft and a careful review. A brief that names the outcome, the audience and the constraints gets you useful work on the first turn instead of three clarifying rounds.
treehouse.lesson.house-collaborate.sched:
Open [Meatbag Tasks](clank://tasks) and create a scheduled practice reminder. Inspect its payload and its run state. When it runs, open its task chat and confirm the answer is there.

**Observable result:** the run produces a committed receipt and the answer appears in that task's own chat. Creating a schedule without a successful run does not count as work done.

You can put the clanker on a schedule. When a scheduled task runs, its answer returns to the original task chat — not to whatever conversation happens to be open. Task identity is preserved so follow-up questions land where the work is.
Cancel the reminder if you do not want it to run; cancellation is safe and reversible.
The task shows its payload and either a committed run receipt or a cancelled status you chose.
Create a one-shot practice reminder and inspect its scheduled payload before it runs.
A scheduled task whose result lands in the chat that owns the task.
Scheduled work and answering in its original task chat
Automation is only useful if its output is findable. A result that answers in the task's own chat keeps the receipt, the transcript and your follow-up in one place.
treehouse.lesson.house-collaborate.tool-:
Open [File access](clank://settings/file-access) and read what is permitted. Then open a chat where the assistant used a tool and expand the tool activity for that turn.

**What is distinctive:** permission is a setting you can read, and activity is a record you can inspect. Neither is hidden in the answer text.

The assistant's reach is bounded by explicit settings. [File access](clank://settings/file-access) states what it may read and write; tool activity in a chat shows what actually ran. Authority is granted in advance, not invented mid-task.
A clear picture of what the assistant may touch and what it just did.
Inspecting tool activity and existing authority
Knowing the boundary before you delegate keeps surprises out of your files. And when something did run, the activity record is how you check it — without guessing from the prose reply.
treehouse.lesson.house-connections.bases:
Open a Base in [Editor](clank://editor). Add a typed value to a practice row and run the view.

**Observable result:** the typed value is returned by the Base query. Text that merely looks like a status is not a typed value.

Bases are live queries over typed document content. Open a Base in [Editor](clank://editor) and it evaluates a filter subset against your documents' properties — status values, topics, dates — and returns matching rows as they change.
Delete the practice row or document when finished.
The Base query returns the row on its typed status value.
A Base that queries typed values and returns the rows that match.
A Base is a view you did not have to maintain. When the property is typed, the query is exact; when the row changes, the view is already current.
treehouse.lesson.house-connections.filte:
In a populated [Graph](clank://graph) view, apply a filter that names a facet and value from the generated facet list, and confirm the result set changes. Then use the camera gestures to zoom and pan.

**Observable result:** the filter changes the result set, and accepted camera gestures change scale by at least 20% and pan at least 48 CSS pixels from the starting camera.

Graph filters are programmatic facets — folder, tag and property values generated from the current corpus — not free text guesses. Camera controls let you zoom and pan a populated view; the controls are ordinary gestures with real effect.
Clear the filter when finished; nothing is deleted.
The result set changes and the camera moves a real distance.
Apply one generated facet/value filter to a populated Graph view.
A filtered Graph view and a camera you actually moved.
Programmatic filters and camera controls in Graph
Filters are how a large house stays navigable. Camera control is how you read one neighbourhood of the graph closely instead of squinting at all of it.
treehouse.lesson.house-connections.graph:
Open [Graph](clank://graph) on a corpus with at least two linked documents. View **Documents · links**, then switch to **Structure · headings and bullets**.

**Observable result:** both modes show at least one actual node. Selecting two empty modes is not enough.

[Graph](clank://graph) has two document modes. **Documents · links** draws the edges between documents. **Structure · headings and bullets** draws the shape inside them. Galaxy is an optional third projection for tracks and events — a related destination, not a replacement for either. (An older name, Mind, referred to structure mode; it is not a separate launcher.)
Delete the practice documents when finished.
Both Graph modes render at least one real node from the practice corpus.
Two linked documents with one heading each, then view both Graph modes.
Both Graph modes mounted on real content, each showing at least one actual node.
Graph: linked-document mode versus structure mode
Links tell you what relates; structure tells you what a document is made of. Switching between them is how you find a missing connection and then find the section that should hold it.
treehouse.lesson.house-connections.links:
In [Editor](clank://editor), create a link from one document to a different document. Follow it. On the target, open the backlink and follow it home.

**Observable result:** the link and its navigation resolve to a different document, and the source and target identities match the edge.
Documents link to each other with ordinary references. Following a link resolves the edge to a real document; the target shows the backlink. Graph treats the same edges as structure you can see.
Delete both practice documents and the link when finished.
Navigation resolves the edge to the other document with matching identities.
Document A links to Document B; follow the edge both ways.
A link followed to its target and a backlink followed home again.
Backlinks are how a note becomes a network. The link you leave in one document is the trail someone else — or future you — follows back.
treehouse.lesson.house-connections.resea:
Open a research note and check that its claims carry source references. Open a Compare result and read the recorded selection and reason.

**What is distinctive:** sources stay attached to the claim, and a comparison leaves a record rather than a vibe. Live inference is optional — recorded fixture responses are enough to learn the workflow, and reading this lesson never starts a paid call.

Research work keeps its sources. A research note records what came from where, so a claim can be checked. Compare sets two recorded responses side by side and records which you chose and why. Both are ordinary content you can open again.
A research note whose claims can be traced to sources, and a Compare result that records why.
Research notes and Compare results with attributable sources
Attribution is what makes research reusable. A conclusion without a source is an opinion; a Compare without a recorded reason is a coin flip you cannot revisit.
treehouse.lesson.house-connections.tasks:
In a document, add a checkbox task and open it in [Meatbag Tasks](clank://tasks). Complete the task and reopen the source document. Separately, create a [Timeline](clank://timeline) event on a practice track and move it to a different date.

**Observable result:** the source checkbox changes from unchecked to checked, and the Timeline event commits and then moves while keeping the same stable event identity.

A task can point at a source document. Completing it changes the referenced checkbox in that document from unchecked to checked — the note and the task stay one piece of work. [Timeline](clank://timeline) holds dated events on tracks; an event can be moved to a different valid date or track and keeps its identity.
Delete the practice note and its Timeline event when finished.
The source checkbox is checked by the task, and the event moves to a new date/track.
One checkbox task in a practice note, and one single-day event on a practice track.
A task that checks a real checkbox in its source document, and a Timeline event you moved.
Work that points back at its source is work you can audit. And a timeline you can reshape is how a plan survives contact with reality without losing its history.
treehouse.lesson.house-documents.images-:
Prepare an image in [Files](clank://files) and insert it into a document in [Editor](clank://editor). Save, reload, and confirm the image still resolves. Then move the document to another folder and confirm the reference remains intact.

**Observable result:** the clipboard image attachment preparation and the document insertion commit together, with an owned asset in the required media location.

Images live in [Files](clank://files) and are inserted into documents through the shared attachment adapter. The document keeps a real reference to the asset: move the document and the known references are checked, not left dangling. Gallery assets are Files assets — there is no separate gallery to manage.
Delete the practice document and its owned image asset when finished.
The image resolves from its Files asset after reload and after a document move.
Insert one small image into a practice document and save.
An image inserted into a document that still resolves to its Files asset after a reload.
Images and links that stay attached to their source
Attachments that survive a reload and a move are what make a document portable. A picture that evaporates when the folder changes is a broken document.
treehouse.lesson.house-documents.new-doc:
Open [Editor](clank://editor) and create a new document. Use the template section inserter to add one supplied section. Edit the inserted text and save.

**Observable result:** the document reopens with your edited section text and the revision marker advanced. The template itself is unchanged.

Create a document in [Editor](clank://editor). Templates are stored in [Settings](clank://settings) and inserting one copies its assets and sections into the document you are writing. Inserting is a copy: editing the inserted section never rewrites the template.
Delete this practice document when you are done, or keep it — it is ordinary content.
The document reopens with the edited section and a newer revision marker.
Create a document and insert one template section; change one line and save.
A document built from a template section, ready to edit.
New documents and insertable template sections
Templates turn the structure you reuse — meeting shape, review checklist, research frame — into something you can drop in without retyping. Because insertion copies, your edits stay yours.
treehouse.lesson.house-documents.rich-ma:
Open a document that contains a supported programming language with a comment or docstring. Render it richly, then use **See source** on the official Markdown Formatting Demo to inspect the source lines behind a block, and return with **Back to rendered**.

**Observable result:** a supported comment or docstring region renders as nonempty Markdown and saves against the source revision. The source-reveal inspector is a formatting-demo feature; ordinary documents keep their own source as the single record.

Editor renders Markdown richly, including comment and docstring regions inside programming source. A **See source** action on the official formatting demo reveals the exact source lines behind each rendered block; on ordinary documents the rendered view and the stored source stay one document.
Delete this practice document when finished.
The docstring region renders as Markdown and the source revision saves.
A comment or docstring over real code, rendered as Markdown and traceable to its exact source.
Rich Markdown and code comments with See source
Documentation that lives with the code is documentation that survives the refactor. Seeing the exact source behind a rendered comment is how you edit it precisely instead of guessing at the Markdown.
treehouse.lesson.house-documents.tabs-an:
Open two documents in [Editor](clank://editor). Split the view so both are mounted at once. In one document, use an in-place link to the other.

**Observable result:** two distinct document panes are mounted simultaneously and the link resolves to the other document. Clicking a split button that is not available does not count.

Editor keeps documents in tabs and can split the view into two panes. In-place links open a document in the other pane rather than replacing what you are reading. Unsaved drafts stay in their buffer while you navigate.
Delete both practice documents when finished.
Two panes are mounted at once and the in-place link opens the second document.
Create two short documents; open both in a split and link one to the other.
Two documents open side by side, with a link that moves between them without losing your place.
Comparison is a real workflow: source and summary, brief and draft, spec and implementation. Splits make it a layout rather than a memory exercise.
treehouse.lesson.house-documents.typed-t:
Open a table in [Editor](clank://editor). Give one column a date type and another a currency type. Add a formula column that totals the currency column. Save and reopen.

**Observable result:** the saved table revision contains a typed date or currency column and a successfully evaluated formula or total.

Tables carry column types: dates, money, plain text and formulas. A typed date or currency column sorts and formats as that type, and a formula column evaluates against the row. Error-valued formulas stay visible as errors — they never quietly become zero.
Delete this practice table when finished.
The saved table revision has a typed date/currency column and an evaluated total.

| Date | Item | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-09-01 | Supplies | 12.50 |
| 2026-09-08 | Filing | 40.00 |

Total formula column: sum(Amount)
A table whose date and currency columns compute a real total.
Typed dates, money and formulas in readable tables
A table that computes is a small model of your numbers. When the total is a formula rather than a typed-in figure, it stays true when the rows change.
treehouse.lesson.house-documents.wiki-wi:
Open the [Wiki](clank://wiki) and create a Wiki-type page. Write a short chunk and link it to another readable document. Reopen the link, then check the backlink on the target.

**Observable result:** the Wiki page commits its Markdown chunk and a valid link/backlink pair with another document.

[Wiki](clank://wiki) has its own page-authoring applet and uses the shared Editor document core. Choose New page, then use Rich formatting or explicit Source view. Wiki pages hold Markdown chunks and link to other documents; the link is real, and the backlink shows up on the target.
Delete this practice page and remove its link when finished.
The Wiki page saves its chunk and a resolving link/backlink to the note.
A short Wiki chunk that links to one existing note.
A Wiki page linked to a note, with shared identity and drafts across Wiki and Editor.
Wiki pages and the shared Editor core
Wiki and Editor share the canonical document buffer, saves, history and attachments. Open in Editor or Open in Wiki changes presentation without copying the page or losing its unsaved draft.
treehouse.lesson.house-making.clipboard-:
Paste an image into a document and inspect where the asset landed in [Files](clank://files). Paste a second image with the same name and observe the collision handling.

**What is distinctive:** the layout is explicit and adoption is protected. Nothing you already own is replaced without you.

Pasting media follows a chosen clipboard layout: the asset lands where the layout says, with an owned name. Adoption of existing material is **protected** — the system will not silently overwrite a file you already have. Collisions surface as a choice, not a surprise.
A pasted image that lands in the right place without overwriting anything.
Clipboard media layout and protected adoption
Media that lands predictably is media you can find later. Protected adoption is why a paste can be trusted near work you care about.
treehouse.lesson.house-making.files-work:
Open [Files](clank://files) and browse. Open the same path from [Editor](clank://editor) and confirm it is the same resource.

**What is distinctive:** Files and Editor share one resource identity. A path is not a copy — it is the same material seen from two places.

[Files](clank://files) is the file tree. A **registered** workspace is one the installation knows about and can manage; a **loose** workspace is ordinary material you pointed at. Both are readable, and Files and Editor share one resource space — the same file is the same file.
A file opened from Files that resolves to the same resource Editor sees.
Files and registered versus loose workspaces
Knowing which kind of workspace you are in tells you what the assistant may do and what recovery can promise. One resource space means no export step just to edit what you can already see.
treehouse.lesson.house-making.imps-layer:
Open an image from [Files](clank://files) in Imps. Add a second editable layer. Save the project and reopen it.

**Observable result:** the project reopens with the same project revision and the same layer identities. To undo the save, restore from the project's history and the preimage replays.

**Imps** is the image editor. A project keeps layers, masks and text as editable structure — not a flattened blob. Saving a managed edit captures a preimage first, so the original is recoverable from the project's history. Gallery assets are Files assets; Imps is where you edit them.
Delete the practice project and its assets from Files when finished.
Reopening shows the same project revision and layer identities.
One image project with two layers: base plus one text or mask layer.
An image project with two editable layers, saved and reopened intact.
Imps layers, masks and text — and original-save recovery
Editable layers are how an image stays useful after the first change. The preimage is why you can experiment: the original is not gone, it is retained.
treehouse.lesson.house-making.lore-resto:
Make a change to a practice document and record a checkpoint. Change it again. From the document's history, restore the retained version.

**Observable result:** the restore commits and the resulting content hash matches the retained version. A digest-only or observed-after claim is not a restore receipt.

Lore retains versions of your work with the receipts needed to restore them. A restore commits a real change: the retained version's content is written back, and the result is confirmed against that version's hash. The restore is itself recorded, so you can go forward again.
Delete the practice document when finished; its history goes with it.
The restore commits and the content hash matches the retained version.
Edit a practice document, checkpoint it, edit again, then restore the checkpoint.
A document version restored from retained history, confirmed by content hash.
A Lore restore on a practice artifact
Recovery you can verify is recovery you can trust. The hash check is the difference between "it seems fine" and "this is the version I chose."
treehouse.lesson.house-making.project-ex:
Export the practice Imps project. Inspect the artifact.

**Observable result:** the export confirms an editable artifact with a valid project manifest and a complete asset set. A bare Export click without a committed artifact does not count.

Exporting an Imps project produces an editable artifact: the project structure plus its assets, with a manifest describing them. Clicking Export is not the result — a committed export with a valid manifest is.
Delete the export artifact when finished if you do not need it.
The export artifact contains a valid project manifest and its asset set.
Export the two-layer practice project and inspect its manifest.
An export artifact with a valid project manifest and asset set.
An editable export is what makes work portable and reviewable. Someone else can open it and see the layers, not just a picture of them.
treehouse.lesson.house-making.scoped-exp:
Export the disposable practice material as a scoped export. Open its manifest and check the contents against what you selected.

**Observable result:** the export finishes and its manifest validation succeeds, attributed to you. A filename on disk alone does not qualify.

A scoped export packages the material you selected and writes a manifest describing exactly what is inside. Reading the manifest is how you confirm the export is complete and nothing extra rode along. Filename existence is not proof.
Delete the export artifact when finished.
The export completes and its manifest validates against the selected scope.
Export only the disposable practice project and read its manifest.
An export limited to what you chose, with a manifest that proves it.
Scoped exports and checking their manifests
Exports are how work leaves the house. A manifest is the packing list — check it and you know what the recipient received.
treehouse.lesson.house-stewardship.app-l:
Follow one shared app link from content in [Editor](clank://editor) and one from TreeHouse content — for example [Settings](clank://settings) and [Graph](clank://graph). Confirm each resolves to an existing app destination.

**Observable result:** two successful shared app-link resolutions, one from Editor content and one from TreeHouse content, each landing on a real destination.

Rich content can link to app screens with `clank://` destinations. A link in [Editor](clank://editor) and a link in TreeHouse use the same resolver: the destination opens and focuses its screen, chat identity is preserved, and unsaved drafts stay in their buffers. A link never toggles an already-open window closed and never starts an unrelated chat.
Delete the practice document when finished.
Both app links resolve to existing destinations without disturbing open drafts.
Place one clank:// link in a practice document and follow one in this lesson.
Two shared app links that open their destinations without disturbing your work.
App links across Editor and TreeHouse
Instructions that take you to the screen they describe are instructions you can follow. One resolver means one behaviour: the link in a lesson and the link in a note work the same way.
treehouse.lesson.house-stewardship.email:
Write a local email draft and create a matching calendar placeholder. Then open [Settings → Integrations](clank://settings/integrations) and inspect webhook status.

**What is distinctive:** drafts and placeholders stay local and inspectable; webhook status is visible before you rely on it. Opening this lesson never sends anything externally.

Email and calendar examples in the Field Guide use **local drafts**. Nothing is sent externally by opening a lesson or writing a draft. Webhooks are an integration: their configuration and delivery status are inspectable in [Settings → Integrations](clank://settings/integrations), and an unconfigured webhook is visibly disabled rather than silently broken.
Delete the draft and placeholder when finished.
The draft and placeholder remain local and inspectable.
One local email draft and one calendar placeholder; no external send.
A local draft and a calendar placeholder that never leave the machine until you send.
Local email and calendar drafts, and webhook status
Drafting locally is how you practise safely. And knowing whether a webhook is actually configured is how you avoid believing an alert went out when nothing did.
treehouse.lesson.house-stewardship.offic:
Open the handbook from Help and read one non-demo page — for example the Open Clank Handbook home — in [Editor](clank://editor). Then open the Markdown Formatting Demo and switch between its rendered view and exact source view.

**Observable result:** an official non-demo documentation page opens by its provisioned identity (a personal folder with a similar name does not qualify), and the formatting demo switches between rendered and source views.

The maintained handbook ships with Open Clank and opens inside [Editor](clank://editor) — there is no separate help browser. Official pages are maintained read-only reference material. The Markdown Formatting Demo shows rendered Markdown and its exact source.
A handbook page opened in Editor, and the formatting demo's exact source view.
Official docs and the formatting demo
Documentation that opens where you work is documentation you will actually read. And a formatting demo with real source reveal teaches Markdown by showing the bytes, not by describing them.
treehouse.lesson.house-stewardship.progr:
Open [TreeHouse](clank://treehouse) and read the achievements view. Note which of your completions were self-checks and which were verified. Mystery entries show `???`; unearned ultra rares are not listed at all. In alpha admin/edit mode, spoilers are visible.

Your account-wide achievements are lifetime records: resetting Class progress does not erase them, and changing workspace does not re-award them.

Progress in the built-in Field Guide is free exploration: any lesson, any order. A lesson marked **self-check** is reading plus your own check; a lesson marked **verified** has an observable persisted result. Completing a lesson is not automatic evidence for an unrelated action award. In the achievements view, mystery entries show `???` until earned and count toward the normal total from the beginning; ultra rares stay absent until earned and appear as a separate `+U` suffix. Alpha admin/edit mode may reveal spoilers.
An honest reading of what you have completed and what is still hidden.
Reading progress, mystery achievements and alpha spoilers

Honest labelling is what keeps achievements meaningful. A self-check is a self-check; a verified practice is something that actually happened. And the secret rules are there so a surprise stays surprising until you earn it.
treehouse.lesson.house-stewardship.teach:
In [TreeHouse](clank://treehouse), create a Class with at least one nonempty lesson. Preview it as a learner, then publish it. Optionally share it with another account.

**Observable result:** your authored Class is previewed as a learner and then explicitly published with at least one nonempty lesson. Seeded official Classes are excluded — this is your own work.

You can author a Class in TreeHouse. Write at least one nonempty lesson, preview it as a learner to see what they will see, then publish. Sharing gives another account access; prerequisites and assessment are features of authored Classes, even though the built-in Field Guide itself is free exploration.
Delete or archive the practice Class when finished.
The authored Class previews as learner and publishes with its nonempty lesson.
One authored Class with a single nonempty lesson.
A Class of your own, previewed as a learner and then published.
Teaching is how you hand over what you learned. The learner preview is the check that the lesson reads the way you meant it to — before anyone depends on it.
treehouse.lesson.house-stewardship.theme:
Open [Settings → Appearance](clank://settings/appearance). Choose a theme and a background effect. Adjust intensity or size if the effect supports them, and set the UI text-size scale where you need it. Reload.

**Observable result:** your owner-scoped theme preference is confirmed and the same values rehydrate after a fresh settings load.

Appearance lives in [Settings → Appearance](clank://settings/appearance) — there is no separate theme applet. Themes change colours across the shell; the picker shows live previews. **Background / Effect** chooses a decorative effect — Solid, Clanker Signal Routes, Shipibo Kene-Inspired Signal Weave, Clanker LCARS, Clanker Gem Drift, Clanker Emoji Drift, Clanker Matrix Rain, Clanker Emoji Rain, Clanker LCARS Status Sweep, Dots, Synapse, Rain, Constellations, Perlin Flow, Petals, Sparkles or Embers — with effect colour, intensity and size where the effect supports them. Typography offers font and density (comfortable, compact, spacious) plus a UI text-size scale. Frosted glass is a toggle.
Change the values back if you prefer; nothing destructive is involved.
The same theme and effect values rehydrate after a new settings load.
Pick a theme and one background effect; note the intensity and size.
A theme and background effect you chose, rehydrating after a reload.
Theme, effect and accessibility controls in Settings
Appearance is not decoration for its own sake — it is how the house stays readable for your eyes. Effects are optional and heavy ones can be turned off without losing the rest of the theme.
treehouse.manifest.field-guide.audience: Assumes basic ChatGPT familiarity; teaches what is distinctive about Open Clank.
treehouse.section.house-explore.descript: Five freely explorable Classes. Jump anywhere; suggested order is only a hint.
treehouse.section.house-explore.title: Explore the House
treehouse.section.house-system.descripti: Hidden system section. Computes aggregate guide state; never rendered as an empty container.

docs.openclank-docs-home.body.compat-e51:
# Open Clank Handbook

Welcome. This is the maintained handbook that ships with Open Clank. It is
read-only: use **Make editable copy** on any page to keep your own notes beside
it. Updates replace these pages in place and never touch your personal copies.

## Start here

- [[Getting Work Done]] — the shape of a normal session
- [[Editor]] — documents, Wiki pages, templates and media
- [[Files and Imps]] — the file tree and managed image projects
- [[Graph]] — how your documents connect

## Your account and tools

- [[Accounts and Models]] — identity, providers and model choice
- [[Chat and Workspaces]] — conversations, drafts and context
- [[Tasks and Continuations]] — turning notes into follow-through

## The rest of the handbook

- [[Memory and Lore]] — what the assistant remembers and how recovery works
- [[Settings and Themes]] — appearance, panels and preferences
- [[Recovery]] — history, backups and when things go wrong
- [[Limits and Platform Support]] — honest capability limits
- [[Markdown Formatting Demo]] — every rendered element with its source

## Go somewhere in the app

These links open the real screen. They never close a window you already have
open and never start a chat on your behalf.

- Open [Settings](clank://settings) or jump to [appearance](clank://settings/appearance)
- Browse [Files](clank://files) or open the [Graph](clank://graph)
- Continue in [Editor](clank://editor) or the [Wiki library](clank://wiki)
docs.openclank-docs-getting-work-done.bo:
# Getting Work Done

Open Clank is a chat-first workspace. You talk with your assistant in the
center, and the Copal suite — Editor, Files, Graph, Timeline, TreeHouse and
Tasks — holds the durable material you produce together.

## A normal session

1. Start or resume a chat. Every conversation keeps its own transcript and its
   own task list.
2. Ask for something concrete. The assistant can read and write your Copal
   documents, run tools, and reference what it did later.
3. Capture the durable parts. Notes, tables, images and tasks live in Copal
   rather than only in the transcript.

Open [Editor](clank://editor) to see the documents, or [Chat](clank://chat) to
return to the conversation.

## Where things live

| You want to | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| Write or read long-form documents | [Editor](clank://editor) |
| Organize linked knowledge pages | [Wiki library](clank://wiki) |
| Manage files and images | [Files](clank://files) |
| See how documents connect | [Graph](clank://graph) |
| Track follow-through | [Tasks](clank://tasks) |
| Change appearance or behavior | [Settings](clank://settings) |

## Two kinds of content

**Personal** notes, copies and annotations belong to you. Rename them, edit
them, delete them — the assistant will not overwrite them just because a name
looks familiar.

**Official** pages like this handbook are read-only and shared by every
account on this installation. They live in the `OpenClank/` folder and update
with the product.

When you want to change an official page, make an editable copy. Your copy is
yours from then on.
docs.openclank-docs-accounts-models.body:
# Accounts and Models

Open Clank is multi-account. Each account owns its own chats, documents, files
and settings, so two people can share one installation without seeing each
other's work.

## Your account

Your account is chosen at sign-in. Documents, tasks, memory and settings are
scoped to that account. If you sign in as someone else you get their
workspace, not yours — nothing is merged.

Local installs without authentication map to a single local account. The
Copal document store is still scoped per owner internally, so enabling
authentication later does not scramble existing data.

## Choosing a model

Models are configured in [Settings](clank://settings/providers). A provider is
the service that runs a model — a local runtime, or a hosted API you bring a
key for.

Practical guidance:

- Pick a small, fast model for quick edits and summaries.
- Pick a stronger model for long reasoning, code or research.
- Switch mid-conversation if a task grows; the transcript keeps both.

Compare is available for side-by-side answers from two models on the same
prompt. It is useful when you are deciding which model to keep.

## What Open Clank does not do

- It does not choose a model for you or silently fall back to a different
  provider without telling you.
- It does not send your documents to a provider unless a tool call or prompt
  needs them.
- It does not store provider API keys in your documents or in first-party
  source.

See [[Limits and Platform Support]] for what runs where.
docs.openclank-docs-chat-workspaces.body:
# Chat and Workspaces

Chat is the conversational surface. Copal is the document surface. They share
one account and one set of resources, but they have different rules.

## Chat

Each conversation is its own transcript with its own history, attachments and
task list. You can keep many conversations open and switch between them from
the sidebar.

Chats can reference Copal documents by name. When the assistant quotes or
links a document, opening that link goes to the document in Editor — it does
not fork the chat or lose your draft.

## Workspaces and drafts

Editor keeps drafts. If you type into a document and navigate away, the draft
is kept and restored when you come back. Saving is guarded: if the stored
version moved underneath you, the save is refused rather than silently
overwriting newer work.

Windows in Copal (Editor, Graph, Timeline and the rest) keep their own
position and selection. Closing a window does not delete anything.

## Identity in links

Document links carry the document identity, not just a title. Renaming a
document keeps its links working. Sharing a link to someone on another account
of the same installation resolves inside their own scope — they see their
copy of the target, not yours.

## Preserving your work

- Drafts survive navigation and window management.
- Answering a task toast resumes in the original task chat, not whichever
  chat happens to be in front.
- Nothing in chat rewrites a Copal document without going through the normal
  guarded save.

Continue with [[Editor]] or [[Tasks and Continuations]].
docs.openclank-docs-editor.title: Editor
docs.openclank-docs-editor.body.compat-7:
# Editor

Editor is the shared document workspace. Markdown pages, Wiki pages, typed
notes, Bases, Canvas, tables and media all open here as typed leaves with
tabs and splits.

## Pages and tabs

Open a document from the file tree or a link. Use tabs for parallel reading,
and splits for side-by-side work. Navigation intent is honored: a normal click
opens in the current tab, Command/Control-click opens a new tab, and the
context menu offers split right or split below.

Links between documents navigate the tab you are in. Explicit new-tab
navigation stays explicit — nothing hijacks your current view.

## Wiki pages

Wiki is a page type inside Editor, not a separate application. The Wiki
library lists your knowledge pages and can create, export and import them as
`.memes` files. Opening a page gives you the article view with links,
backlinks and details — the same tabs, splits and save ownership as any other
document.

Wikilinks look like `[[Some Page]]`. Existing targets open on click; missing
targets are shown as broken links you can create. Backlinks on a page list
every page that points at it.

See the [Wiki library](clank://wiki) or open [Editor](clank://editor).

## Templates

Templates live in a folder you choose in
[Settings](clank://settings). Inserting a template copies its assets and
links into the current document and keeps resource identity, so attachments
stay attached.

## Source comments

Rich source comments attach a comment to a range of the document source. They
travel with the document and survive edits outside the range. Comments are
part of the document record, not a separate overlay store.

## Media and attachments

Images, audio, video and PDFs can be attached to a document or referenced by
path. Embedded media renders inline in the Markdown view. Attached files are
owned by the document and move with it.

The [[Markdown Formatting Demo]] shows every formatting element this renderer
supports, with its raw source one click away.
docs.openclank-docs-formatting-demo.body:
# Markdown Formatting Demo

reveal the exact Markdown source that produced it. The source inspector is
read-only — you can select and copy from it, but it never edits this page and
never starts a save. Use **Back to rendered** to return.

## Headings

### A level-three heading

#### A level-four heading

## Emphasis and marks

Some **bold text**, some *italic text*, some ~~struck-through text~~, and some
==highlighted text==.

Inline `code spans` look like this.

## Lists

- First bullet
- Second bullet

- Third bullet

1. First step
2. Second step
3. Third step

## Task list

- [x] A finished item

## Quote

> It can span more than one line.

## Code

```
  return 'world';

```

## Rule

## Table

## Links and references

A [standard link](clank://settings) opens a real app screen.

A wikilink target such as [[Editor]] opens another document in this Editor.

## Footnote-style note
